uv --version

QEMU can use software emulation inside a RouterOS container. KVM acceleration requires an accessible /dev/kvm and host support; installing quickchr does not grant it. Size lab storage and memory for both T3 and any guest routers.

Image-owned Bun packages live in /opt/bun; user bun install --global packages live in /data/.bun. PATH searches /data/.local/bin, /data/.bun/bin, then /opt/bun/bin before system tools. User-installed overrides persist and take precedence after an image upgrade. Build arguments BUN_VER, QUICKCHR_VER, and CENTRS_VER can select specific releases instead of the defaults.

Good upstream navigators (pingdotgg/t3code docs):

  • install / requirements (t3 serve, providers) — install.md
  • remote access (t3 up, --lan, T3 Connect relay, pairing) — remote-access.md
  • background service (memory/OOM guidance, t3 service) — background-service.md
  • telemetry opt-out — telemetry.md
  • project settings / storage cleanup — project-settings.md
  • FAQ (disk usage is worktree cleanup) — faq.md

The image only documents one requirement: an installed, authenticated provider. There are no published CPU/RAM minimums; size from your workload (agents + browser), not from a datasheet.

Tags

Images track upstream stable T3 Code releases only — no nightlies (CI still accepts any T3CODE_VER input for one-off builds):

  • ghcr.io/tikoci/app-t3code:0.1.7 — exact release
  • ghcr.io/tikoci/app-t3code:0.1, :0, :latest — stability aliases
  • ghcr.io/tikoci/app-t3code:0.1.7-app.<N> — one promoted build, never moved. N is the ci workflow's run number. PR and branch runs use numbers too, so promoted builds skip some. A re-run that rebuilds appends the attempt (-app.<N>.2). Pin this to stay on a build; CHANGELOG.md headings use the same name.
  • ghcr.io/tikoci/app-t3code:sha-<commit> — the candidate CI pushes from main; not for deployment

Each pushed image carries its build name in the OCI label org.opencontainers.image.version (and the commit in org.opencontainers.image.revision), so a sha- candidate that never got promoted still says which run built it.

A main push publishes only the candidate. Its arm64 image then runs the container replacement test natively on a GitHub arm64 runner (amd64 already ran it before the push), and only then does CI move the release tags onto the same manifest, by digest. A failed arm64 run leaves :0.1 where it was, and a run that finishes after main has moved on skips promotion, so the tags never go back to an older build.

The /app YAML references the :0.1-style stability tag, and test/app-yaml.test.ts fails the build if it drifts from package.json's major.minor. Bumping T3 versions = bump T3CODE_VER (default in Dockerfile + Makefile), package.json, and the YAML tag together.

Developing

bun install
bun run check          # biome + tsc --noEmit + markdownlint
make lint              # check, plus hadolint/ShellCheck and actionlint (need them on PATH)
bun run test           # offline, Linux only: YAML contract, payloads, installers
make freshness         # needs network: upstream T3, Claude download contract, share link
APP_T3CODE_INTEGRATION=1 bun test test/integration/
# Build the image, then prove the tools and container-replacement persistence:
docker build -t app-t3code:test .
APP_T3CODE_DOCKER_IMAGE=app-t3code:test bun test test/container-replacement.test.ts

The integration test boots a real CHR per arch with @tikoci/quickchr@next, drives it with @tikoci/centrs@next, and asserts the web UI answers with the expected serverVersion:

APP_T3CODE_ROS=stable APP_T3CODE_ARCH=arm64 APP_T3CODE_INTEGRATION=1 \
  bun test test/integration/

The Docker replacement test removes the original container and starts a new one with only the same home volume. Every container sets its selection explicitly, except one that checks the image default. It installs the dev, capture, labs, vpn and routing payloads under all, runs each Debian group's tools as the unprivileged user (capture, labs, vpn, routing), and relinks the payloads in later containers, including with no network, then relinks the image default offline and checks that none leaves only core. Against an emulated (QEMU user-mode) image, set CAPTURE_TOOLS_QEMU_USER=1, ROUTING_TOOLS_QEMU_USER=1 and/or LABS_TOOLS_QEMU_USER=1 for the test; they are forwarded to the scripts, which then skip only the checks emulation breaks (or makes too slow) before any permission check. It checks tool discovery in ordinary and login shells, a real T3 project record and environment identity, settings (including the restarted server's effective preference through read-only MCP), uncommitted worktree/project files, a user-installed Bun CLI, provider configuration in the home, and that a user-installed muse in /data/.local/bin wins on PATH. CI runs this against the built x86 image before publishing, and builds both image architectures. It does not authenticate providers or run paid model requests.

Hands-on CHR runs (install, /app/update with an offline /data backup, commands inside the container, before/after manifests of the home) follow .agents/skills/chr-app-lab, and their results are in docs/notes/ (dated run logs and closeouts; topic research is in docs/research/). They have confirmed that /app/update keeps /data (projects, threads, settings, logins, tool payloads and the environment ID). Assigning /app/set yaml= to an installed app does not: it wipes the app-owned volume, even for a comment-only change.

Both helpers float on next on purpose: if a helper breaks, report it to centrs / quickchr instead of working around it silently. CI (ci.yml) lints, tests, builds both arches, runs the replacement test on amd64 (every build) and natively on arm64 (main and dispatch only), then promotes the tags (see Tags); integration.yml runs the CHR matrix weekly and on demand (against :0.1), and after each successful main publish (against that commit's :sha-<commit> candidate, via APP_T3CODE_IMAGE).

The pages.yml workflow publishes only tracked *.md, *.tikapp.yaml, and *.tikappstore.yaml files, preserving their paths and contents. Automatic deployments run only when those files change on main; manual dispatch is also available. Pages must use GitHub Actions as its publishing source in the repository's Settings → Pages. No site generator is used.

Verified install flow on CHR 7.25 (x86, free license):

  1. first-boot deviceMode: { enable: ["container"] } → rose mode (the guest-side /system/device-mode/update never completes);
  2. installPackage("container") (/app 404s without the package);
  3. /disk/format <id> file-system=ext4 (7.25 has ext4, no ext3), then /app/settings/set disk=<mount-point>;
  4. api … app -X PUT -f yaml=… -f use-https=no --yes (colon-style 3773:3773:web:tcp ports parse as firewall-redirects);
  5. /app/set … disabled=no (PUT leaves the app disabled:true);
  6. poll /app + /container (.running is the string "true") + GET /.well-known/t3/environment → serverVersion.

The routeros-app-yaml, routeros-container, routeros-tikoci-centrs, routeros-tikoci-quickchr-cli and tikoci-crossref skills govern this repo; AGENTS.md has the working notes.

Security and changes

SECURITY.md covers how to report a vulnerability, the trust boundaries (RouterOS access implies container access), the startup pairing token in /container/log, and what installs at runtime. CHANGELOG.md lists the user-visible changes in each promoted build.

License

MIT — see LICENSE.
dockerfileContent:
# tikoci/app-t3code — RouterOS /app container for T3 Code.
#
# Rebuilds the wodby/t3code approach from our own Dockerfile so the image we
# ship on GHCR is one we control: Debian trixie-slim (glibc, which the T3 Code
# release binaries need), per-arch t3 tarball from pingdotgg/t3code with
# SHA256 verification, the GitHub CLI, uv/uvx and Bun/RouterOS tools baked
# in. No provider CLI is baked: the T3CODE_PROVIDERS selection (#13) installs
# Claude Code, Codex and the others into the volume in the background.
#
# Build:
#   docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
#     --build-arg T3CODE_VER=0.1.7 -t ghcr.io/tikoci/app-t3code:0.1 .
# Run (plain HTTP on 3773; terminate TLS in front for remote use):
#   docker run -p 3773:3773 -v t3code:/data -e PUBLIC_URL=https://t3.example.com ghcr.io/tikoci/app-t3code:0.1

ARG NODE_VER=24
ARG BUN_VER=1.4.4
ARG UV_VER=0.13.7

FROM oven/bun:${BUN_VER}-slim AS bun

# Astral's multi-arch distroless image carries only the static uv and uvx.
FROM ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:${UV_VER} AS uv

FROM node:${NODE_VER}-trixie-slim AS runtime

ARG TARGETARCH
ARG T3CODE_VER=0.1.7
ARG QUICKCHR_VER=next
ARG CENTRS_VER=next
ARG GH_VER=2.103.3

ENV T3CODE_VER="${T3CODE_VER}"
ENV T3CODE_HOST=0.0.0.0
ENV T3CODE_PORT=3773
# RouterOS `/app/set environment=` replaces the whole env list, so anything
# the /app YAML sets must also be an image default here (issue #5).
ENV T3CODE_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false
# Optional tool groups (lib/tool-catalog.ts DEFAULT_TOOL_GROUPS): an
# explicit list, so a group added later is never enabled silently. Operators
# remove names, or set `none` for core only, with /app/set environment=.
ENV T3CODE_TOOL_GROUPS="capture labs vpn routing dev"
# Provider CLIs to install into the home (lib/providers.ts
# DEFAULT_PROVIDERS): an explicit list, like the groups above. OpenCode, Pi,
# Grok and Muse are opt-in; Cursor and Antigravity come with T3 itself.
ENV T3CODE_PROVIDERS="claude codex"
# uv uses the image's Python 3 and never fetches a managed Python by itself;
# `uv python install` still works when asked for explicitly.
ENV UV_PYTHON_DOWNLOADS=manual

ENV SHELL=/bin/bash
# A failed download or checksum grep must fail its pipe, not only the last
# command (hadolint DL4006).
SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-o", "pipefail", "-c"]

# Browser dependencies for T3 Code's built-in browser, which downloads itself
# on first use. They are core, not an optional group: T3 starts its browser
# itself, so the libraries stay where the system loader finds them.
# `t3 browser setup` cannot run at build time: it needs the browser
# downloaded first and fails on build hosts that restrict user namespaces.
# (Same set as upstream wodby/t3code.)
RUN echo 'Acquire::Retries "10";' > /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/80-retries && \
    apt-get update && \
    DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
        bash \
        ca-certificates \
        curl \
        git \
        jq \
        less \
        make \
        openssh-client \
        procps \
        python3 \
        ripgrep \
        unzip \
        fontconfig \
        fonts-liberation \
        libasound2t64 \
        libatk-bridge2.0-0t64 \
        libatk1.0-0t64 \
        libatspi2.0-0t64 \
        libdbus-1-3 \
        libexpat1 \
        libgbm1 \
        libglib2.0-0t64 \
        libnss3 \
        libx11-6 \
        libxcb1 \
        libxcomposite1 \
        libxdamage1 \
        libxext6 \
        libxfixes3 \
        libxkbcommon0 \
        libxrandr2 && \
    apt-get clean && \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* /var/cache/apt/archives/*

COPY --from=bun /usr/local/bin/bun /usr/local/bin/bun
# Scope the image's global install to /opt. Runtime Bun installs instead use
# the persistent user's /data/.bun, which precedes these tools on PATH.
RUN ln -s bun /usr/local/bin/bunx && \
    BUN_INSTALL=/opt/bun bun install --global \
        "@tikoci/quickchr@${QUICKCHR_VER}" \
        "@tikoci/centrs@${CENTRS_VER}" && \
    rm -rf /root/.bun/install/cache

# Python bootstrap: uv for project environments, uvx for one-off Python CLIs.
# Tools, caches and venvs land in the home (/data/.local, /data/.cache/uv), so
# they survive image replacement; a uv the user installs in /data/.local/bin
# wins on PATH.
COPY --from=uv /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/

RUN usermod --home /data --shell /bin/bash node && \
    mkdir -p /data && \
    chown node:node /data

# Release downloads land in /tmp and are removed in the same layer.
WORKDIR /tmp

RUN set -eu; \
    if [ -z "${T3CODE_VER}" ]; then \
      echo "T3CODE_VER is required (example: 0.1.7)"; \
      exit 1; \
    fi; \
    case "${TARGETARCH}" in \
      amd64) arch=x64 ;; \
      arm64) arch=arm64 ;; \
      *) echo "Unsupported architecture ${TARGETARCH}"; exit 1 ;; \
    esac; \
    archive="t3-${T3CODE_VER}-linux-${arch}.tar.gz"; \
    url="https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/releases/download/v${T3CODE_VER}"; \
    curl -fsSL --retry 3 -O "${url}/${archive}"; \
    curl -fsSL --retry 3 -O "${url}/SHA256SUMS"; \
    grep -E "[[:space:]]*?${archive}$" SHA256SUMS | sha256sum -c -; \
    mkdir -p /opt/t3code; \
    tar -xzof "${archive}" --strip-components=1 -C /opt/t3code; \
    rm -f "${archive}" SHA256SUMS; \
    ln -s /opt/t3code/t3 /usr/local/bin/t3

# RouterOS pairing help (#18): one <script> tag in the upstream client's
# index.html loads client/routeros-pairing.js, which adds the RouterOS token
# command under T3's pairing form. No other upstream file changes. The script
# fails the build, rather than shipping a pairing screen without the help,
# when the index.html shape or the form's #pairing-token id changes upstream.
COPY client/routeros-pairing.js scripts/install-pairing-help.sh /tmp/pairing-help/
RUN sh /tmp/pairing-help/install-pairing-help.sh /opt/t3code/client /tmp/pairing-help/routeros-pairing.js && \
    rm -rf /tmp/pairing-help

# GitHub CLI: T3's GitHub source-control provider and agents' pull-request
# work need `gh`. Release tarball checked against the release's checksums
# file. Its login (`gh auth login`, or GH_TOKEN) lives in /data/.config/gh.
# Other forges' CLIs (glab, fj/tea, ...) are not bundled; see issue #15.
RUN set -eu; \
    case "${TARGETARCH}" in \
      amd64|arm64) ;; \
      *) echo "Unsupported architecture ${TARGETARCH}"; exit 1 ;; \
    esac; \
    name="gh_${GH_VER}_linux_${TARGETARCH}"; \
    url="https://github.com/cli/cli/releases/download/v${GH_VER}"; \
    curl -fsSL --retry 3 -O "${url}/${name}.tar.gz"; \
    curl -fsSL --retry 3 -O "${url}/gh_${GH_VER}_checksums.txt"; \
    grep -E "[[:space:]]${name}\.tar\.gz$" "gh_${GH_VER}_checksums.txt" | sha256sum -c -; \
    tar -xzof "${name}.tar.gz"; \
    install -m 0755 "${name}/bin/gh" /usr/local/bin/gh; \
    rm -rf "${name}" "${name}.tar.gz" "gh_${GH_VER}_checksums.txt"

WORKDIR /

# Core network tools (issue #5 assignment, see README "Network tool
# assignment"), the sqlite3 CLI and zstd (bin/install-claude-code downloads
# Claude's .zst build: about 99 MiB instead of 280). Small user-space clients
# only; capture, VPN and routing peers belong to optional groups. A separate
# late layer keeps the heavy layers above cacheable when this list changes.
RUN apt-get update && \
    DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
        bind9-dnsutils \
        ethtool \
        freeradius-utils \
        iperf3 \
        iproute2 \
        iputils-ping \
        mosquitto-clients \
        mtr-tiny \
        netcat-openbsd \
        snmp \
        socat \
        sqlite3 \
        traceroute \
        whois \
        zstd && \
    apt-get clean && \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* /var/cache/apt/archives/*

# Everything that must survive a restart lives in the home directory on the
# volume: T3 Code's database, agent logins, projects, and tools the user
# installs. Tools installed there with npm or a native installer win over the
# image's copies.
ENV HOME=/data
ENV T3CODE_HOME=/data/.t3
ENV NPM_CONFIG_PREFIX=/data/.local
# Tool-group payload shims (issue #5) follow the user's own installs, so a
# tool the user installed wins; a project's node_modules/.bin wins via npx.
ENV PATH="/data/.local/bin:/data/.bun/bin:/data/.local/share/t3code-tools/bin:/opt/bun/bin:${PATH}"

COPY docker-entrypoint.sh /
COPY bin /usr/local/bin
COPY profile.sh /etc/profile.d/t3code.sh
# lib/ is the shipped runtime (AGENTS.md "Layout"); scripts/ never ships.
COPY lib /usr/local/lib/t3code

# Native tool groups (`capture`, `vpn`, `routing`, `labs`) install as
# Debian-package payloads into the home at runtime, as node. QEMU and its
# firmware are not in the image: `labs` brings them (quickchr stays above).
# Pin each group's dependency closure (whatever this image lacks) by version,
# size and SHA256 from apt's verified indexes now, so a rebuild picks up
# Debian security updates and the payload id follows them.
# Must stay after every apt layer: the closure is computed against them.
# HOME=/root: Bun run as root would otherwise seed a root-owned /data/.bun.
RUN apt-get update && \
    HOME=/root bun /usr/local/lib/t3code/deb-lock.ts && \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

RUN install -d -o node -g node /usr/share/t3code/inventory

USER node

WORKDIR /data

# Capture the completed image before the entrypoint installs anything into HOME.
RUN bun /usr/local/lib/t3code/image-inventory.ts --output /usr/share/t3code/inventory && \
    t3code-tools status --json --groups all > /usr/share/t3code/inventory/tool-groups.json && \
    for lock in /usr/local/lib/t3code/groups/*/debs.lock.json; do \
      group="${lock%/debs.lock.json}"; \
      cp "$lock" "/usr/share/t3code/inventory/${group##*/}-debs.lock.json"; \
    done

VOLUME /data

EXPOSE 3773

# T3 Code runs many agent processes: t3code-init (bash) reaps them and
# forwards signals. Not tini: RouterOS sends SIGTERM only to a PID 1 that has
# a handler installed for it, and SIGKILLs tini at once (#25).
ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/t3code-init", "/docker-entrypoint.sh"]

CMD ["t3", "serve"]

# Export inventories for both architectures without loading/running the ARM
# image on the CI host. Keep the default target as the runnable image below.
FROM scratch AS inventory
COPY --from=runtime /usr/share/t3code/inventory/ /

FROM runtime AS final

name: centrs
description: Multi-protocol (REST, native API, mac-telnet, SSH) CLI and TypeScript interface to RouterOS, with rich help and validation
readmeHtml:
centrs

centrs is the tikoci RouterOS interaction hub: a Bun/TypeScript library and CLI (with an MCP server; TUI and HTTP proxy frontends planned) for talking to MikroTik RouterOS devices through a regularized, validated interface.

Stable releases are published on npm under latest. To try the offline analyzer without installing centrs or connecting to a router:

bunx @tikoci/centrs@latest explain '/ip/address print' --json

Use bunx @tikoci/centrs@latest --help to inspect the release CLI, and bunx @tikoci/centrs@latest --version (-V; --json for an envelope) to print the exact version for scripts and field reports. The dist-tag follows standard SemVer semantics: a plain version (0.1.10) publishes to latest and carries next forward with it, while a next build (0.1.11-next.23) publishes to next only and never moves latest. A next build is described by the next version's ## X.Y.Z — next section of CHANGELOG.md. So @next is the leading edge and can equal @latest between cuts — npm view @tikoci/centrs dist-tags is the authority.

The full flag reference for every command is generated from the CLI metadata into docs/CLI.md; per-command behavior lives in commands/<name>/README.md.

It is a friendly conduit, not a high-level configuration abstraction. It helps humans and agents reach RouterOS over the right protocol, with the right credentials and ports, and validates RouterOS-shaped commands before running them. It does not hide RouterOS behind helpers like createVlanOnBridge() — you still speak RouterOS. Validation and structured diagnostics are the product; without them this would just be a worse curl.

Status: early npm preview under active development. It is not production-ready: expect bugs and breaking changes before 1.0, and exercise router-writing workflows on lab or disposable targets first. Offline explain does not contact a router, but its analysis is intentionally conservative and never proves that RouterOS will accept a command at runtime. Check current dist-tags with npm view @tikoci/centrs dist-tags --json. The library, device registry, and first MCP server phases are CHR-verified; the CLI is wired (coded); encrypted-CDB reads and writes are supported, and the TUI/proxy frontends are planned. docs/MATRIX.md is the single source of truth for what works today — treat anything not green there as not-yet-shipped. The 0.1.10 known issues cover MAC-Telnet output loss (#575) and the MCP authorization race during concurrent CDB edits (#604).

What it talks to, and how

  • Frontends: TypeScript API, CLI, MCP server (Phase 1 + first Phase 2 CDB mutation CHR-passed — see commands/mcp/), TUI and HTTP proxy/daemon (future).
  • Protocols: REST API and native API for reads and writes; SSH / MAC-Telnet for execution and interactive terminals; SFTP for file transfer; MNDP for discovery; bandwidth test for peer measurement. RoMON and WinBox Terminal are planned. centrs picks the protocol for you (and lets you pin one with via= or --via).
  • Commands: every router-facing command resolves a target — a router you name on the CLI — to a real address, credentials, and a protocol, then runs. (Local commands — devices, settings, discover, and explain's offline mode — need no router.)
Command Purpose
retrieve Read RouterOS state over REST/native API. --follow keeps a menu's rows current over native API (snapshot, then a line per change; NDJSON); --sample <interval> re-reads it on a timer for counters; --query filters on the router with the print where grammar; --wait retries until a read succeeds (or an optional --until condition holds), up to a deadline.
execute Run RouterOS CLI-shaped read/write commands (add/set/remove) over native API, REST, SSH or MAC-Telnet.
api Structured RouterOS API passthrough (gh-api style): one command per operation, structured in/out, can write, over REST or native API. Follow changes with api … <menu>/listen; --stream streams any command's replies (native API; NDJSON).
terminal Open an interactive console, primarily SSH or MAC-Telnet.
transfer Upload, download and manage device files over REST/native API or SFTP; upload and download are shortcuts.
btest Run a MikroTik bandwidth-test client or server over TCP/UDP.
check Probe reachability and management protocol availability. Designed, not implemented — see docs/MATRIX.md.
explain Analyze RouterOS source offline, or add read-only device evidence over REST/native API, including path schemas, completion candidates and value types. Runtime acceptance remains unproven.
devices View and maintain the CDB-backed device registry (the only writer).
discover Discover MNDP neighbors and optionally save them into the CDB.
settings Manage centrs's global preferences (centrs.env) and inspect the __default__ record. Interactive first-time setup is planned.

Each command's commands/<name>/ directory carries its design and the executable example list that gates "done".

Your WinBox address book is the device registry

centrs deliberately has no separate credential vault or inventory database. Instead it piggybacks on the one most RouterOS admins already keep: the WinBox connection database (CDB), the winbox.cdb file that WinBox writes when you save a router in its address book.

Global preferences live in centrs.env, managed by settings; device records and saved credentials stay in the CDB. See the settings contract.

centrs reads (and, through devices, writes) that same file at its well-known location, ~/.config/tikoci/winbox.cdb (override with --cdb-file / CENTRS_CDB_FILE). From each saved entry it takes the fields WinBox already stores:

  • target — the address you saved (IPv4, IPv6, MAC, or DNS name); a literal you can type at the CLI to reach the box. centrs also resolves a <router> against three sanctioned comment lookup keys — identity=, mac=, and ip= — so a router whose target is 192.0.2.5 is still reachable as edge1 when its comment carries identity=edge1. Every other comment token stays inert prose. See commands/devices/README.md (Identity model) for the full resolution rules.
  • user / password — the credentials centrs connects with. They stay in the CDB. devices show / add / set withhold the password and report passwordSet (--show-password reveals it); MCP results/resources always redact it.
  • group and port — used for selection and connection settings. profile and session are preserved for WinBox compatibility; centrs does not act on them.

So centrs retrieve edge1 /ip/address works with no flags: edge1 is looked up in the CDB, its credentials and address come along for the ride. A target that isn't in the CDB still works, but then --username / --password (or CENTRS_USERNAME / CENTRS_PASSWORD) become mandatory.

Overloading the comment: per-device settings as key=value

A WinBox CDB entry has no field for "always use SSH for this box" or "skip validation here" — those are centrs concepts WinBox knows nothing about. Rather than invent a parallel store, centrs overlays its own settings onto the one free-text field WinBox does have: the comment. It parses key=value tokens (the "comment kv-soup") out of that free text and treats the recognized ones as per-device defaults. Everything else in the comment stays inert human prose.

A comment like:

edge1 prod border router   via=ssh validate=false mcp=rw

leaves edge1 prod border router as plain text for you and WinBox, while centrs reads three settings from it. The recognized keys:

Key Effect
via Default transport for this device (rest-api, native-api, ssh, …).
validate true / false. false is the escape hatch; a CLI flag still wins.
timeout Default request timeout in ms (per-transport caps still apply).
port Non-default transport port.
www-port, www-ssl-port, api-port, api-ssl-port, ssh-port Per-service port, named after /ip/service. Only the matching transport reads it (REST, native API, SSH); it beats port, which applies to every transport.
ssh-key Path to a per-device SSH private key (a path only — never key material).
source Provenance marker for discovered/imported records (mndp, dude, …).
mcp MCP write policy: ro (default) or rw. See below.

The first-class fields WinBox already stores (user, password, group, profile, session) must not be written into the comment — they have real CDB tags, and devices set refuses to put them there. Unknown keys produce a cdb/unknown-option warning and are ignored, so a stray = in human prose never breaks anything.

Settings resolve lowest-to-highest: built-in defaults → user config file (centrs.env) → comment-kv → CENTRS_* env → CLI flag / API arg. Every result envelope reports which source won each setting under meta.settings, so you can always see why a given port or transport was chosen.

Groups, discovery, and the MCP allowlist all ride on the CDB

  • Groups are CDB-native: an entry's group field is just a string, and --group prod-edge fans a single command out to every entry that shares it. There is no separate group-definition file. Groups are one selector in a uniform fan-out grammar shared by api, retrieve, execute, and transfer: mix <router> positionals, repeatable --group/--where <attr>=<value>, --all, and --default (de-duped by CDB record index). Every fan-out returns the locked FanoutData envelope (per-target results, not metadata) with a granular exit code (0 all ok / 2 partial / 1 all failed); a multi-target write is gated once by --yes naming the blast radius. See docs/CONSTITUTION.md (Target selection grammar).
  • CMR fleets (RouterOS 7.26beta1+) are selected on the controller instead: execute <controller> --cmr --labels <expr> -- '<command>' validates the command on each client through CMR and runs it there, using only the controller's credentials. See commands/execute/README.md (CMR).
  • Discovery writes back into the CDB: discover --save records MNDP neighbors as new entries tagged group=discovered with a source=mndp marker — hints to curate, not authoritative inventory.
  • The MCP server uses the CDB as its authorization boundary. The allowlist checks that a target exists in the CDB; RouterOS write-shaped execution requires the entry to carry mcp=rw plus per-call confirmation. centrs_devices can also add/set/remove CDB records in-band, and centrs_discover can save MNDP neighbors, with confirm: true. The allowlist and the write policy are the same CDB data you already manage — see commands/mcp/. Concurrent CDB edits can invalidate the checked record before dialing (#604); see the security policy.

devices owns CDB mutations, including those requested through MCP or discover --save. Record mutations use a cross-process lock, a loaded-revision check, timestamped backups (two retained by default), and atomic rename, preserving unknown WinBox fields verbatim. High-level library mutations reject stale LoadedCdb snapshots with cdb/conflict. The low-level writeWinBoxCdb() requires expectedRevision to enable locking and revision checks; omitting it skips both protections. devices init uses atomic no-clobber creation instead. CLI/MCP add, set and remove operations and discover --save reload and retry. Close WinBox before mutating the same file: external writers do not take the centrs lock. Encrypted-CDB reads and writes work with --cdb-password / CENTRS_CDB_PASSWORD; writes decrypt, mutate and re-encrypt with a fresh salt. devices init --encrypt creates an encrypted registry, and devices encrypt explicitly converts an existing open CDB. Conversion retains existing backups and warns that plaintext copies remain. The manual WinBox round-trip is still pending; see the per-command contract for the current evidence and limits. The full contract — identity resolution, ambiguity handling, write strategy, and the comment grammar — lives in commands/devices/README.md and docs/CONSTITUTION.md (Identity and CDB).

The result envelope, validation, and errors

  • Validation is on by default (validate=true). CLI-shaped execute and api /execute scripts pass the offline analyzer before device validation. Reads are checked through /console/inspect; CLI-shaped commands through [:parse]. Set validate=false (per device or per call) only as a deliberate escape hatch.
  • Every call returns one envelope: { ok, data?, warnings, tips, error?, meta }, with provenance and source-of-truth reporting in meta.
  • Errors are typed values, not thrown strings, with slash-namespaced codes (routeros/…, transport/…, validation/…, cdb/…) and a details_url of the form https://tikoci.github.io/centrs/errors/<code> for the human-readable explanation.

The load-bearing contract — envelope shape, error model, protocol selection, settings precedence, and the "done" definition — lives in docs/CONSTITUTION.md. Capability status, the current track and parked themes, including the command×protocol grid and offline analysis, live in docs/MATRIX.md.

Repository layout

For contributors. An admin only needs the CLI and their CDB; this is where the code and authority docs live.

  • docs/CONSTITUTION.md — load-bearing rules (validation, envelope, error model, settings precedence, identity/CDB, protocol selection, done).
  • docs/MATRIX.md — capability status, the current track, parked themes and nits (the command×protocol grid plus offline analysis and frontend surfaces); the only status surface.
  • commands/<name>/ — per-command README and executable examples.
  • src/ — Bun/TypeScript source.
  • test/ — unit and CHR-backed integration tests.

There is no docs/specs/, no work/, no roadmap doc. The matrix and the GitHub issues it links are the roadmap.

Development

Requirements:

  • Bun 1.4.4 or newer within 1.x (engines.bun: >=1.4.4 <2; CI runs the packageManager version in package.json; Bun 2.x not yet validated).
  • Git.
  • uv, only for bun run lint:actions (zizmor workflow audit).
  • For integration tests: QEMU plus @tikoci/quickchr (handles CHR image download and boot).
bun install
bun run lint
bun run test
bun run test:integration   # CHR-backed; required before claiming "done" on transport code
bun run test:integration:long-term  # channel-specific CHR gate
bun run build

Generated API docs through TypeDoc:

bun run build:doc:api

The explain censuses measure a RouterOS script corpus that lives in tikoci/lsp-routeros-ts, not in this repo. scripts/corpus-pin.json records which snapshot centrs measures against — a commit plus the blob's sha256 — and corpus:fetch downloads and verifies it. A sibling lsp-routeros-ts checkout is used when present, and the censuses print the source and hash they used:

bun run corpus:fetch          # download the pinned snapshot, verify its sha256
bun run explain:corpus-census # genre census (#203)
bun run explain:value-census  # value-surface census (#225)

Done definition (short version)

Live capabilities require every applicable example in commands/<name>/examples.md green on real CHR via bun run test:integration. Offline analysis requires its command README's full baseline acceptance criteria, including committed CHR-grounded semantic evidence. The fixture-backed devices and settings integration suites retain their command-specific contracts. Full rule: docs/CONSTITUTION.md → Done definition.

COPY package.json bun.lock ./

name: quickchr
description: `quickchr` - Fastest path to MikroTik RouterOS CHR instance for testing and scripts -– agent ready, human friendly
readmeHtml:
quickchr

CLI and library to download, launch, and manage MikroTik CHR virtual machines via QEMU.

Quick Start

Prerequisites

  • Bun runtime, 1.4.3 or newer
  • QEMU with qemu-system-x86_64 and/or qemu-system-aarch64
  • qemu-img for default qcow2 creation, the setup wizard, disk resize, extra disks, and snapshots
  • UEFI firmware (edk2) for arm64 CHR

Install QEMU:

# macOS
brew install qemu

# Ubuntu/Debian
sudo apt install qemu-system-x86 qemu-system-arm qemu-efi-aarch64 qemu-utils

# Fedora/RHEL
sudo dnf install qemu-kvm qemu-system-aarch64 edk2-aarch64 qemu-img

# Arch
sudo pacman -S qemu-full
# Windows — install QEMU (qemu-img is included)
winget install SoftwareFreedomConservancy.QEMU

# Install Bun (PowerShell — matches bun.sh official install docs)
powershell -c "irm bun.sh/install.ps1 | iex"
# Alternative: winget install Oven-sh.Bun

Running in a Claude Code cloud session or another proxied sandbox with no KVM? See MANUAL.md → Claude Code cloud sessions for the network access and setup script it needs.

Install

CLI:

bun install -g @tikoci/quickchr
quickchr doctor

Library:

bun add @tikoci/quickchr

Prerelease QA (0.5.1)

0.5.1 is published to npm next first; the unqualified install above uses latest, and 0.5.1 is promoted there once QA passes. Pin this published candidate for reproducible CLI or library QA:

bun install -g @tikoci/quickchr@0.5.1
bun add @tikoci/quickchr@0.5.1
quickchr --version

Use @next instead of @0.5.1 to follow later candidates. See the 0.5.1 changelog for the changes since 0.5.0, including storage admission, cache accounting, and disk preservation fixes. The 0.5.0 notes cover migration from 0.4.x.

CLI Usage

The easiest way to start is the interactive wizard — it walks through every option and starts the CHR for you. It requires qemu-img and reports a missing tool before prompting or downloading:

quickchr setup

Or run quickchr with no arguments on a TTY to get the same wizard automatically. See MANUAL.md §3 setup for a step-by-step breakdown of every wizard prompt.

All wizard options are also available as flags for scripting:

# Create a machine without starting it
quickchr add --name my-chr --channel stable --arch arm64

# Create with a resized boot disk and extra blank disks
quickchr add --name lab --boot-size 1G --add-disk 512M --add-disk 2G

# Start an existing machine
quickchr start my-chr

# Create and start in one step
quickchr start --name throwaway --version 7.22.1 --boot-size 2G

# List instances (table view)
quickchr list

# Detailed status for one instance
quickchr status my-chr

# Stable connection descriptor/env for a running instance
quickchr inspect my-chr
quickchr env my-chr
quickchr env my-chr --json

# Stop an instance
quickchr stop my-chr

# Stop all instances
quickchr stop --all

# Run a RouterOS CLI command on a running instance
quickchr exec my-chr /system/resource/print
quickchr exec my-chr ":put [/system/routerboard/get serial-number]"

# Attach to serial console of a running instance (exit: Ctrl-A X)
quickchr console my-chr

# Tail QEMU log
quickchr logs my-chr
quickchr logs my-chr --follow

# Query live machine config (license, device-mode, admin users)
quickchr get my-chr
quickchr get my-chr license
quickchr get my-chr device-mode --json

# Manage snapshots (requires qcow2 boot disk)
quickchr snapshot my-chr list
quickchr snapshot my-chr save before-upgrade
quickchr snapshot my-chr load before-upgrade
quickchr snapshot my-chr delete before-upgrade

# Apply or renew a trial license
quickchr license my-chr

# Network discovery and virtual socket management
quickchr networks
quickchr networks sockets

# Set up shell completions (bash/zsh/fish)
quickchr completions

# Persist a default so you stop repeating a flag on every add/start
quickchr settings set default-channel long-term
quickchr settings set secure-login true
quickchr settings print

# Resolve/cache an image without creating or booting a machine
quickchr cache key --channel stable
quickchr cache add --channel stable --arch x86

# Reset disk to fresh image
quickchr clean my-chr

# Inspect disk layout
quickchr disk lab

# Remove instance entirely
quickchr remove my-chr

# Check prerequisites
quickchr doctor

quickchr stop <name> terminates QEMU (a power cut). For an explicit guest shutdown request, use quickchr shutdown <name> [--timeout <seconds>] (default 10 seconds, or QUICKCHR_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT). It waits for QEMU to exit and clearly reports a forced power cut if the guest does not stop within the grace budget.

Create / Start Options

Flag Description Default
--version <ver> RouterOS version (e.g., 7.22.1) Latest stable
--channel <ch> stable, long-term, testing, development stable
--arch <arch> arm64, x86, or auto Host native
--name <name> Instance name Auto-generated
--cpu <n> vCPU count 1
--mem <mb> Memory in MB 512
--boot-disk-format <f> Boot disk format: qcow2|raw qcow2
--boot-size <size> Resize boot disk (e.g., 512M, 2G). Requires qemu-img.
--add-disk <size> Attach an extra blank qcow2 disk. Repeatable. Requires qemu-img.
--forward <spec> Add or pin a QEMU SLiRP hostfwd mapping. Repeatable.
--no-wait Return once QEMU is running; readiness is up to the caller. Not with provisioning flags or --fg
--fg / --foreground Run in foreground — serial console on stdio
--bg / --background Deprecated, does nothing — background is already the default. Warns; use --no-wait to return early
--add-package <pkg> Extra package to install (repeatable)
--install-all-packages Install all packages from all_packages.zip
--add-user <user:pass> Create a user after boot
--disable-admin Disable the default admin account
--secure-login Create a managed login; use --disable-admin to disable admin
--no-secure-login Keep admin with no password (skip managed account creation)
--add-network <spec> Add a network NIC (repeatable). Specs: user, shared, bridged:<iface>, socket::<name>, tap:<iface>. Default: single user NIC.
--no-network Start with no NICs (headless)
--no-winbox Exclude WinBox port mapping
--no-api-ssl Exclude API-SSL port mapping
--license-level <l> Apply trial license: p1, p10, unlimited
--license-account <a> MikroTik account email env MIKROTIK_WEB_ACCOUNT
--license-password <p> MikroTik account password env MIKROTIK_WEB_PASSWORD
--device-mode <m> Configure device-mode: rose|advanced|basic|home|auto|skip
--device-mode-enable <f> Set one or more device-mode flags to yes
--device-mode-disable <f> Set one or more device-mode flags to no
--no-device-mode Skip device-mode provisioning entirely
--port-base <port> Starting port number Auto (9100+)
--timeout-extra <s> Add extra seconds to the auto-computed boot timeout
--dry-run Print what would run without executing

RouterOS Provisioning Support Policy

quickchr separates boot-only machine management from post-boot provisioning.

  • Boot-only / QEMU-local features work on older RouterOS 7.x builds: image download, boot/start, disk resize, extra disks, network attachment, and port mappings.
  • Post-boot provisioning is validated/tested on RouterOS 7.20.8+ only: package install, managed login or custom user creation, disabling admin, CHR license operations, and device-mode changes.
  • This is a quickchr support policy, not a RouterOS claim that older versions can never work. We intentionally stop at the first long-term baseline to avoid version-specific provisioning traps that are not covered by tests.
  • If you plan to provision, prefer --channel long-term or an explicit version >= 7.20.8.
Feature Minimum RouterOS Notes
Boot / start / stop Any RouterOS 7.x; RouterOS 6 on x86 (best-effort) Boot-only path; no post-boot RouterOS mutations. 6.x has no REST: readiness is a native-API login, and provisioning is refused — see MANUAL "RouterOS 6 (boot-only)"
Disk resize / extra disks / disk inspection Any RouterOS 7.x Requires host qemu-img; QEMU-local only
Network attachment / port mappings Any RouterOS 7.x QEMU networking setup; not provisioning
Managed login / custom user / disable-admin 7.20.8+ Post-boot provisioning
Package install / install-all-packages 7.20.8+ Post-boot provisioning
License apply / renew 7.20.8+ Post-boot provisioning
Device-mode changes 7.20.8+ Post-boot provisioning; intentionally unsupported below the baseline

Background vs Foreground Mode

By default quickchr start runs QEMU in the background: QEMU is spawned as a detached process and the command returns once CHR has booted. Use quickchr list, quickchr status, and quickchr stop to manage it.

# Background (default) — returns after CHR finishes booting
quickchr start --channel stable

# Foreground — serial console attached to your terminal
quickchr start --channel stable --fg

In foreground mode, your terminal becomes the CHR serial console. Use these key sequences:

Key Action
Ctrl-A X Exit QEMU and return to shell
Ctrl-A C Toggle QEMU monitor (quit to force-stop)
Ctrl-A H List all key shortcuts

Note: Background QEMU processes are true OS-level orphans — quickchr does not use shell job control (&). After the command returns you can close the terminal and QEMU keeps running. quickchr stop <name> ends it with a power cut; quickchr shutdown <name> asks the guest to shut down first, and still falls back to a power cut if it does not exit in time.

Disk Support

  • CLI and wizard boot disks default to qcow2, converted from the raw MikroTik image using qemu-img. Library callers default to raw unless bootSize implies qcow2.
  • --boot-size resizes qcow2 before first boot; explicitly combining raw with a boot size is refused.
  • Extra disks from --add-disk are always created as blank qcow2 images.
  • quickchr clean <name> removes any resized boot disk and extra disks, then recreates them from the saved machine config.
  • quickchr disk <name> shows the stored disk layout. If qemu-img is installed, it also shows virtual and actual sizes.
  • quickchr snapshot manages qcow2 internal snapshots (requires a qcow2 boot disk).

Multi-NIC Networking

By default each CHR gets a single user-mode NIC (SLIRP). Use --add-network to add more NICs or replace the default:

# Two CHRs on a shared L2 segment via socket_vmnet (macOS) or bridge (Linux)
quickchr start --name router1 --add-network user --add-network shared
quickchr start --name router2 --add-network user --add-network shared

# Named virtual socket (L2 link between two CHRs; either may start first)
quickchr networks sockets create lab-switch
quickchr start --name r1 --add-network socket::lab-switch
quickchr start --name r2 --add-network socket::lab-switch

# More than two machines on one segment needs UDP multicast, which does not work
# on macOS or where UDP is blocked — and fails silently when it does not
quickchr networks sockets create lab-segment --mode mcast

# Bridge to a physical interface
quickchr start --name gw --add-network user --add-network bridged:en0

Not sure which mechanism fits your traffic (host→guest service, host receiving guest-originated UDP, L2 broadcasts, VM↔VM links, real LAN)? See the networking recipes guide — a "traffic shape → mechanism" decision table. The CLI flags map 1:1 to the library: --add-network ↔ StartOptions.networks, --forward ↔ StartOptions.extraPorts.

Port Layout

Each instance gets a block of 10 ports. With the default base of 9100, the first instance maps:

Offset Service Default port
+0 HTTP / REST / WebFig 9100
+1 HTTPS 9101
+2 SSH 9102
+3 RouterOS API 9103
+4 RouterOS API-SSL 9104
+5 WinBox 9105
+6–+9 Reserved (spare) 9106–9109

The second instance gets 9110–9119, and so on.

Custom Port Forwards and Fixed WinBox

Use --forward <spec> on add or create-and-start start commands to add extra QEMU SLiRP hostfwd mappings. The shorthand uses the built-in service registry when it knows the guest port:

quickchr add lab --forward smb                  # auto host port → guest 445/tcp
quickchr add dude-lab --forward winbox:8291     # host 8291 → guest WinBox 8291/tcp
quickchr add app-lab --forward myapp:9200:7777/udp
quickchr add btest-lab --forward btest:9200-9210:2000-2010/udp  # UDP port range

A port range (name:hostStart-hostEnd[:guestStart-guestEnd][/proto]) expands to one hostfwd per port — handy for L3 peers with dynamic data ports. To receive UDP a guest sends (no forward at all), see the gateway path in the networking recipes guide.

Reusing a built-in service name such as winbox pins/replaces that service's host port for the machine. Existing machines keep the mapping stored in machine.json; recreate the machine to change fixed service ports cleanly.

Machine Descriptors and Subprocess Environments

quickchr inspect <name> [--json] emits a stable, versioned (descriptorVersion: 1) JSON descriptor for a running machine — the quickchr ↔ centrs interface contract (issue #71, docs/centrs-interface.md): status, machine identity, and a per-service services map (rest-api, native-api, ssh) giving host/port/transport/tls/availability/auth for each, plus optional customForwards and networks. --json is accepted for parity; inspect output is always JSON. It has no env field — use quickchr env for subprocess env vars.

quickchr env <name> [--json] prints the same subprocess environment as ChrInstance.subprocessEnv(): shell KEY=value lines by default, or a JSON map with --json.

Credential caveat: descriptor/env output includes connection secrets — subprocessEnv()/quickchr env's QUICKCHR_AUTH/BASICAUTH, and each descriptor() service's own auth fields (services["rest-api"].auth.password/ .basic/.header; services["native-api"].auth.password, no basic/header; services.ssh.auth.privateKeyPath) — so child processes can connect without reading quickchr's secret store. Treat it like a password: do not commit it, paste it into public issues, or leave it in CI logs. Stopped machines fail with MACHINE_STOPPED; start the machine before requesting a descriptor or env map.

Library Usage

import { QuickCHR } from "@tikoci/quickchr";

// Start a CHR instance
const chr = await QuickCHR.start({
  name: "disk-lab",
  channel: "stable",
  arch: "arm64",
  mem: 512,
  bootSize: "1G",
  extraDisks: ["512M", "2G"],
});

// Use REST API
const info = await chr.rest("/system/resource");
console.log(info);

// Run a RouterOS CLI command
const result = await chr.exec("/system/resource/print");
console.log(result);

// Stop (or remove)
await chr.stop(); // power cut for normal teardown
// Alternatively, replace stop() above with: await chr.shutdown({ timeoutMs: 10_000 });
await chr.remove();

console.log(chr.state.bootDiskFormat); // "qcow2"
console.log(chr.state.extraDisks);     // ["512M", "2G"]

Version & channel API

Pick which CHRs are worth booting (handy for CI matrices) without scraping CLI text:

import { resolveActiveChannels, resolveAllVersions } from "@tikoci/quickchr";

await resolveAllVersions();
// { stable: "7.23.1", "long-term": "7.21.4", testing: "7.23rc4", development: "7.24beta2" }

await resolveActiveChannels();
// ["stable", "long-term", "development"]
//   released channels always, plus any pre-release at/ahead of stable

compareRouterOsVersion orders pre-release suffixes (7.24beta2 < 7.24rc1 < 7.24 < 7.24.1). The same map is available from the CLI via quickchr version --json. See MANUAL.md → Version & channel helpers.

Cache API

CI can resolve cache identity and download an image without booting QEMU:

import { CACHE_VERSION_UNRESOLVED, cacheAdd, cacheKey } from "@tikoci/quickchr";

const identity = await cacheKey({ channel: "stable", arch: "x86" });
// { dir: "/home/runner/.local/share/quickchr/cache", version: "7.24.4", arch: "x86" }

if (identity.version !== CACHE_VERSION_UNRESOLVED) {
  await cacheAdd({ version: identity.version, arch: "x86" });
}

An explicit version never performs channel resolution. Offline channel lookup returns version: "unresolved" from cacheKey; cacheAdd remains strict and fails when it cannot resolve or download the requested image.

Use in Tests

import { describe, test, afterAll, expect } from "bun:test";
import { QuickCHR } from "@tikoci/quickchr";

let chr: Awaited<ReturnType<typeof QuickCHR.start>>;

test("boot CHR and check version", async () => {
  chr = await QuickCHR.start({ channel: "stable" });

  const resource = await chr.rest("/system/resource");
  expect(resource["board-name"]).toContain("CHR");
}, 120_000);

afterAll(async () => {
  if (chr) await chr.remove();
});

Environment Variables

Variable Description
MIKROTIK_WEB_ACCOUNT MikroTik.com account email (for license renewal)
MIKROTIK_WEB_PASSWORD MikroTik.com password (for license renewal)
QUICKCHR_DEFAULT_CHANNEL, QUICKCHR_DEFAULT_ARCH, QUICKCHR_ACCEL, QUICKCHR_CACHE_MAX_SIZE, QUICKCHR_STORAGE_RESERVE, QUICKCHR_TIMEOUT_EXTRA, QUICKCHR_SECURE_LOGIN Env-tier overrides for the 7 quickchr settings keys — see MANUAL.md §3 settings
QUICKCHR_INTEGRATION Set to 1 to run integration tests
QUICKCHR_TEST_TARGET Integration tests only: RouterOS channel (stable/long-term/testing/development) or pinned version (e.g. 7.22.1) to boot. Empty = stable. The Integration workflow resolves each routeros-target once, then sets this to that exact pin across platforms

The full list (including QUICKCHR_DATA_DIR, QUICKCHR_NO_PROMPT, QUICKCHR_DEBUG, NO_COLOR) is in MANUAL.md §11.

Documentation

  • MANUAL.md — complete reference: every CLI command, every library API, provisioning, channels, networking, storage, errors. Source-checked.
  • examples/ — runnable scripts (bun run): quickstart/ (boot + query), grounding/ (apply config → read back — the one bun:test), dude/ (install a package), harness/ (drive an external tool), rollback/, service-forward/, file-transfer/, device-mode/, plus mndp/udp-gateway/ version-matrix. See examples/COVERAGE.md.
  • docs/networking-recipes.md — which networking mechanism for which traffic shape.
  • DESIGN.md — architecture, layers, design principles.
  • CONTRIBUTING.md — dev setup and bun run check.
  • CHANGELOG.md — release history.

Using quickchr with an AI agent? The routeros-quickchr skill (in tikoci/routeros-skills) teaches agents the grounding workflow — boot a CHR, apply config, read it back — plus the networking recipes and harness patterns.

name: routeros-skills
description: Custom instruction SKILL.md for MikroTik RouterOS v7
readmeHtml:
MikroTik RouterOS "SkillStore" (SKILL.md) for AI assistants

Custom instruction skills for GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Codex, and similar AI coding assistants that teach them about MikroTik RouterOS v7.

Skills

Names distinguish RouterOS knowledge from tikoci tooling:

  • routeros-*: RouterOS features, protocols, and platform knowledge.
  • routeros-tikoci-*: using public tikoci tools with RouterOS, including centrs and quickchr. Future tikoci tool skills use this prefix too.
  • Bare tikoci-*: local project and maintainer skills, outside this repository.
Skill Description
routeros-fundamentals RouterOS v7 domain knowledge — CLI, REST API, scripting, architecture. The foundational skill that others build on.
routeros-scripting RouterOS scripting and CLI config automation — .rsc syntax, [find] selectors, script-safe IDs, arrays, globals, scheduler policies.
routeros-container RouterOS /container subsystem — VETH/bridge networking, OCI images, device-mode, lifecycle management.
routeros-firewall RouterOS firewall filter, NAT, mangle, and address-list configuration — rule ordering, connection tracking, address/interface lists, DNS redirects, and port forwarding.
routeros-hotspot RouterOS hotspot captive portal for wired/wireless access control — hotspot chains, profiles, walled garden, DHCP option 114 (RFC 8910), RADIUS integration.
routeros-app-yaml RouterOS /app YAML format for container applications (7.21+ builtin, 7.22+ custom YAML).
routeros-command-tree /console/inspect API — command tree introspection, schema generation, CLI-to-REST mapping.
routeros-syntax-inspection /console/inspect syntax surfaces (highlight/completion/syntax) + :parse IL — validating commands, reading token streams, enum discovery, script "explain"/lint; necessary-not-sufficient vs runtime.
routeros-qemu-chr MikroTik CHR (Cloud Hosted Router) with QEMU — boot, VirtIO, acceleration, CI/CD patterns.
routeros-tikoci-quickchr Ground RouterOS config/scripts/API code against a real router with quickchr (@tikoci/quickchr) — boot a disposable CHR, apply config, read it back; networking recipes, integration-test harness patterns.
routeros-tikoci-quickchr-cli The shell-first half of quickchr — boot a disposable CHR from the terminal and drive it with centrs. Lifecycle (add is not start), --bg, endpoints and credentials, L2 links between VMs, and the provisioning steps that only apply before first boot.
routeros-tikoci-centrs Drive a real router or CHR with centrs (@tikoci/centrs) — target resolution from the WinBox CDB or a quickchr VM, RouterOS command validation before it runs, and one structured envelope over REST, native API, SSH/SFTP, MAC-Telnet, and MNDP. Use instead of hand-rolled curl/ssh.
routeros-zerotier Native ZeroTier on ARM/ARM64 — instances, network authorization, RouterOS controllers, managed routes, firewall integration, RoMON, and bridging.
routeros-webfig Link humans to RouterOS WebFig views — connections, addresses, VLANs, bridges, firewall rules and CMR; object URLs, login/session behavior, and native WebView integration guidance grounded on CHR browser checks.
routeros-netinstall netinstall-cli for automated RouterOS device flashing — etherboot, BOOTP/TFTP, modescript.
routeros-proprietary-protocols Navigator for MikroTik-specific protocols and file formats — WinBox/M2, MAC-WinBox, RoMON, MAC-Telnet, MNDP, API, EoIP, btest, IP packing, and binary files; research/implementation pointers and explicit knowledge gaps.
routeros-mndp MNDP (MikroTik Neighbor Discovery Protocol) — wire format, /ip/neighbor, WinBox discovery.
routeros-mac-telnet MAC-Telnet (UDP 20561) — Layer-2 terminal by MAC address, 22-byte header, control blocks, MD5 + MTWEI (EC-SRP) auth.
routeros-sniffer RouterOS packet capture and TZSP streaming — /tool/sniffer, firewall sniff-tzsp, Wireshark integration.

Install

Clone this repo and symlink the skill folders into your assistant skill directories:

git clone https://github.com/tikoci/routeros-skills.git ~/GitHub/routeros-skills

cd ~/GitHub/routeros-skills
make link   # Copilot, Claude, Codex, and Hermes
make check

The centrs and quickchr skills were renamed to routeros-tikoci-*. Existing installs should run make link after pulling, update explicit skill names and links, and start a fresh assistant session. See migration details.

Each skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file and optionally a references/ subfolder. VS Code Copilot and Claude Code automatically discover skills in their respective ~/.*/skills/ directories. Codex discovers user-authored skills in ~/.agents/skills, and Hermes in ~/.hermes/skills.

Tip: Start with routeros-fundamentals — it covers the core concepts that other skills reference.

Repository layout

This repo is the single source of truth for all routeros-* skills. Locally, ~/.copilot/skills/routeros-*, ~/.claude/skills/routeros-*, ~/.agents/skills/routeros-*, and ~/.hermes/skills/routeros-* are symlinks into this repo — editing any of those locations is the same as editing here.

Non-routeros-* skills (e.g. tikoci-*, screenshot, sql-as-rag) are personal/project-scoped and live only in the local user-level skill directories, not in this repo. See SETUP.md for the full local setup guide.

The Skill Set is the routeros-*/ folders only. Everything else at the repo root is the CI/QA and tooling layer that validates and ships those skills — it is not part of the skill content and is not symlinked into ~/.*/skills/:

  • .github/ — CI workflows (lint, link check, dependency review), CodeQL Default Setup, and Dependabot config
  • scripts/ — the SKILL.md validator (check-skills.ts) run by CI and make lint
  • hooks/ — optional local git hooks that re-symlink skills after checkout/merge (make install-hooks)
  • Makefile, .markdownlint*.yaml, cspell.json, project-words.txt, package.json, bun.lock — lint/build configuration and the dev dependency tree

Scope

These skills cover RouterOS 7.x (long-term and newer releases). RouterOS v6 is not covered and accuracy for v6 questions will be low.

Contributing

  1. Fork this repository (or branch, if you have write access)
  2. Edit or add skills (each skill is a <name>/SKILL.md folder)
  3. Run the checks locally: make lint (and make lint-links if you have lychee)
  4. Open a pull request — main is protected, so all changes land via PR

Every PR is gated by CI (markdownlint + cspell + a SKILL.md validator + offline link check) and reviewed by CodeRabbit and Copilot. See CONTRIBUTING.md for the local setup, the dictionary policy, and what each check does.

Feedback, corrections, and new skill ideas are welcome via issues.
